stories.title: Sherwood Offloads Hudson Yards Condo Tower Site to Joyland Management for $100M
stories.excerpt: Joyland Management has dropped $100 million on a 17,275-square-foot residential development site in Manhattan’s Hudson Yards neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. The site at 460 10th Avenue was sold by Sherwood Equities, which acquired the property in the early 1990s in anticipation of Hudson Yards’ redevelopment, according to its website. Sherwood planned to build more than 200 residential units on the site, as well as retail space and underground parking. In February, Sherwood filed plans with the Department of Buildings to increase the project’s size by nearly 70,000 square feet, CO reported, in exchange for the addition of affordable housing and $11.8 million worth of improvements to the neighborhood’s infrastructure. JLL Capital Markets’ Jonathan Hageman, Ethan Stanton, Andrew Scandalios, Hall Oster, Michael Mazzara and Brendan Maddigan represented Sherwood in the sale, while it’s unclear who repped the buyer, as well as why Sherwood offloaded the site. The large lot between West 35th and West 36th streets is currently occupied by a 63-space parking lot. It’s unclear what Joyland’s exact plans are for the development project, but the site offers 247,797 square feet of maximum zoning floor area, according to JLL, including 228,053 square feet of residential floor area and 19,744 square feet of commercial or retail space. This isn’t Joyland’s first time buying a notable development project in the city. In January, the firm acquired the stalled hotel and residential project at 159 Broadway in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, from former lender Madison Realty Capital for $30 million, CO reported at the time. Joyland later filed plans to build a new 12-story, 99-unit mixed-use building on the site. Spokespeople for Joyland and Sherwood did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sherwood Equities sells Hudson Yards site (460 10th Ave) to Joyland for $100M.
Site holds entitlements for 200+ units plus 70k SF expansion pending affordable housing.
Sherwood exits after 30+ years, reason unclear; signals potential financing or market timing pressure.
stories.summary: Sherwood Equities offloaded a 17,275-sf residential development site at 460 10th Avenue in Manhattan's Hudson Yards to Joyland Management for $100 million. The property carried entitlements for more than 200 units, retail, and parking; Sherwood had filed to add nearly 70,000 sf in exchange for affordable housing contributions and $11.8M in infrastructure improvements. The sale reason is undisclosed, but exits after three decades of land assembly suggest possible capital reallocation or market headwinds.
stories.impact: Hudson Yards multifamily pipeline now in hands of new operator; timing of exit amid affordable housing requirement complexity (485-x wage mandates) may signal developer caution on hard costs or financing certainty. Watch whether Joyland accelerates or delays the project—an exit before major pre-dev spend flags underwriting stress in Manhattan's high-cost development environment.

stories.title: Retail Media Networks: Different Strategies for Different Shoppers
stories.excerpt: Retail media networks continue to develop, Placer.ai reports in a new white paper. In many stores, advertisements on screens, on personal devices, or over audio have become a regular part of the shopping trip. “For the brands buying that in-store retail media space, getting ROI on their ad spend begins with a few simple questions that shape every media plan: who are the shoppers, when do they visit, how long do they stay for, and how often do they come back,” reports Placer.ai in the new white paper, titled 3 Brands, 3 Retail Media Playbooks. Using the latest location intelligence, the report examines three leading retailers with media networks (Kroger, Sam’s Club, and CVS) to reveal what drives their strategy and what sets them apart: Each brings something different to the table. For example, Kroger Precision Marketing spans more than a dozen grocery banners that can draw very different audiences, Placer.ai reports. At Sam’s Club, ads now appear via a whole new channel: fuel-pump screens. The post Retail Media Networks: Different Strategies for Different Shoppers appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Retail media networks (Kroger, Sam's Club, CVS) driving in-store advertising strategies.
No direct multifamily demand, supply, capital, or cost impact identified.
Tangential: tenant mix and retail sales health may influence mixed-use development demand.
stories.summary: Placer.ai whitepaper examines how leading retailers with media networks (Kroger Precision Marketing, Sam's Club fuel-pump ads, CVS) tailor advertising strategies to shopper behavior—timing, frequency, dwell time, demographic targeting. Each retailer deploys different tactics based on audience composition and visit patterns.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Indirectly, retail media growth may improve co-tenancy desirability and NOI stability for mixed-use projects with grocery or club anchors, but no supply, demand, or capital signal for apartment-only builders.

stories.title: 99-Unit Buildings Accounted for a Third of Proposed NYC Multifamily Projects in Q3
stories.excerpt: You’d be hard pressed to find someone in New York City’s real estate world with mostly positive things to say about the 485-x tax abatement program. The initiative replaced the old 421-a tax abatement program and was designed to encourage more affordable housing development across the five boroughs. But 485-x’s generous wage requirements for construction workers on projects with 100 or more units — one of the biggest critiques facing the program — has been a stumbling block for the city’s affordable housing developments. Between July 2024 and September 2026, the Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY) found there were 172 proposals for 99-unit buildings in New York City, 49 of them appearing in the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)’s prospective 485-x registration data and 123 appearing in the Department of Buildings’ (DOB) new building filings. By comparison, only 13 buildings with exactly 99 proposed units were filed with the DOB from 2008 through 2023, REBNY found. During the third quarter of 2026, REBNY found that 47 proposals for 99-unit buildings were filed with the DOB, which represents 4,653 apartments, or 31.6 percent, of the total 14,712 proposed multifamily apartments filed during the period. Broken down by borough, in the third quarter there were 18 plans for 99-unit building projects registered with the DOB in Brooklyn, 16 in the Bronx, 12 in Queens, one in Manhattan, and zero in Staten Island, according to the REBNY data. “New York cannot meet its housing needs by building small,” Basha Gerhards, executive vice president of public policy at REBNY, said in a statement. “We need policies that make it possible to build substantially more housing, particularly in transit-rich neighborhoods that can support greater density. With the city estimating that 700,000 new homes are needed over the next decade, we should be encouraging larger projects and making sure every neighborhood contributes to addressing the housing crisis.
bullets: 172 proposed 99-unit buildings filed July 2024–Sept 2026 in NYC; 47 in Q3 alone (4,653 units).
485-x wage requirements for 100+ units driving developers to cap projects at 99 units.
Sharp pivot from 2008–2023 baseline: only 13 prior 99-unit filings citywide vs. ongoing 99-unit surge.
stories.summary: NYC developers filed 172 proposals for exactly 99-unit buildings between July 2024 and September 2026—49 with HPD's 485-x program, 123 with DOB—compared to just 13 such filings from 2008–2023. In Q3 2026 alone, 47 buildings with 99 units were filed, totaling 4,653 apartments. The 485-x affordable housing tax abatement's steep prevailing-wage requirement for projects with 100+ units is the stated culprit, forcing developers below that threshold to avoid wage mandates.
stories.impact: 485-x is artificially capping project density and creating a supply-side perverse incentive in NYC. Developers are optimizing for unit avoidance rather than neighborhood need, fragmenting sites and increasing per-unit infrastructure/soft costs. This signals regulatory failure: the affordable housing mandate is pricing out scale projects and may ultimately reduce total supply. Underwriters and acquisitions teams must stress-test underwriting on wage liability overhang and monitor whether HPD/DOB close the loophole or accept permanent density loss.

stories.title: High Street Logistics Properties Picks Up 300K-SF Logistics Facility in Tolleson
stories.excerpt: High Street Logistics Properties acquired a 302,640-square-foot cross-dock distribution facility located at 9704 West Roosevelt Street in Tolleson, Arizona. The building, known as the Palo Verde Distribution Center, sits on 13.83 acres and includes roughly 8,000 square feet of office space. Strategically positioned near the interchange of Interstate 10 and Loop 101 in Phoenix’s Southwest Valley, the property is 100% leased to two tenants, California Closets Fulfillment and Tom Auto Parts, with a weighted average lease term of 8.0 years. Built in 1984, the facility features 30-foot clear heights, 40-foot by 40-foot column spacing, and an ESFR sprinkler system. The secured site includes 32 dock-high doors and four grade-level doors. The Cushman & Wakefield team of Phil Haenel, Will Strong, Foster Bundy and Madeline Warren represented both parties in the transaction. Cushman & Wakefield’s Mike Haenel, Andy Markham, and Justin Smith provided leasing advisory services. Phoenix’s Southwest Valley continues to demonstrate strong industrial market fundamentals, recording 14.4 million square feet of leasing activity through Q3 2026, the highest three-quarter total on record for the submarket, according to Cushman & Wakefield research. The post High Street Logistics Properties Picks Up 300K-SF Logistics Facility in Tolleson appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: High Street Logistics buys 302k-SF cross-dock in Tolleson, Arizona (Phoenix SW Valley) for undisclosed price.
100% leased, 8-year WAULT; tenants: California Closets Fulfillment, Tom Auto Parts.
SW Valley logged record 14.4M SF leasing Q1–Q3 2026; strong industrial fundamentals.
stories.summary: High Street Logistics Properties acquired the Palo Verde Distribution Center, a 302,640-sf cross-dock facility in Tolleson, Arizona (I-10/Loop 101 interchange, Phoenix SW Valley), on 13.83 acres. The 1984-built asset is 100% leased with 8.0-year weighted average lease term to California Closets Fulfillment and Tom Auto Parts. Phoenix's SW Valley recorded 14.4M sf of leasing activity through Q3 2026—the highest three-quarter total on record.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily signal. Industrial market heat in Phoenix SW Valley reflects strong e-commerce/fulfillment demand and logistics hub momentum; this may draw logistics workforce and add job density to the submarket, eventually supporting multifamily demand in secondary/tertiary locations near freeway corridors. Monitor for ancillary residential development (workforce housing) near industrial clusters.

stories.title: Fort Collins Affordable Housing Community Refinanced with $17.2M HUD Loan
stories.excerpt: Johnson Capital Multifamily LLC (JCM) and Gershman Investment Corp have arranged a $17.2-million HUD-insured refinancing for Caribou I & II, a 193-unit affordable multifamily community in Fort Collins, Colorado. The loan was completed through HUD’s Section 223(f) program and carries a 35-year term. The mortgage will be funded through the issuance of Ginnie Mae mortgage-backed securities. Caribou I & II is a Class B, garden-style apartment community located at 4135 Verbena Way in Fort Collins. The property was developed in two phases, with the first completed in 2008 and the second in 2013. The property is approximately five miles from downtown Fort Collins and is near major healthcare facilities, retail destinations, parks and public transportation. The community was developed utilizing 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credits. Phase I includes 96 rent- and income-restricted units at 40% and 50% of Area Median Income, while all 96 units in Phase II are restricted at 30%, 40%, 50% and 60% of AMI. The post Fort Collins Affordable Housing Community Refinanced with $17.2M HUD Loan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JCM/Gershman arrange $17.2M HUD 223(f) refi for Caribou I & II, Fort Collins (193 units).
35-year term, Ginnie Mae MBS; garden-style Class B built 2008–2013.
Affordable units (30%–60% AMI); near downtown, healthcare, retail, transit.
stories.summary: Johnson Capital Multifamily and Gershman Investment Corp completed a $17.2-million HUD Section 223(f) refinancing for Caribou I & II, a 193-unit affordable multifamily community in Fort Collins. The loan carries a 35-year term and will be securitized via Ginnie Mae MBS. The garden-style Class B property was developed in two phases (2008 and 2013) with 9% LIHTC; units are rent-restricted at 30%–60% of Area Median Income.
stories.impact: HUD 223(f) refi activity in secondary markets signals ongoing liquidity for stabilized affordable assets and long-term tax-credit deals. For Trammell Crow, this underscores capital availability for hold/refi plays in mid-market metros like Fort Collins; however, 35-year fixed rates and Ginnie Mae securitization reflect the government's commitment to permanent affordable supply, crowding out conventional equity-backed development in affordable segments. Monitor HUD rate trends as a leading indicator for mixed-income development underwriting in similar markets.

stories.title: AI Startup Aaru Commits to Expansion in NYC
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence startup Aaru has committed to creating 650 jobs in New York City over the next five years, Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office announced. The company will lease and build out more than 27,000 square feet of office space near Union Square, growing its workforce from about 60 employees today to more than 700. The location has not yet been disclosed. Aaru co-founder and CEO Cameron Fink said, “We made a deliberate decision to build Aaru in New York City. The depth and diversity of talent here, proximity to the world’s largest enterprises, and the city’s history of innovation make it the right place for what we’re building.” The new jobs will span software engineering, computer and information research, product development, enterprise sales, client management, and corporate operations. The state has offered Aaru up to $13.12 million in performance-based Excelsior tax credits in exchange for 650 jobs and $109 million in research and development expenditure commitments. The post AI Startup Aaru Commits to Expansion in NYC appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Aaru AI startup commits to 650 jobs, 27k+ SF near Union Square in NYC over 5 years.
Workforce expands 60 → 700 employees; state offers $13.12M Excelsior tax credits.
Roles span engineering, R&D, sales, ops; $109M R&D spend commitment tied to incentive.
stories.summary: AI startup Aaru committed to creating 650 jobs in New York City and leasing/building out 27,000+ sf of office space near Union Square over five years, growing from ~60 to 700 employees. New York State offered up to $13.12 million in performance-based Excelsior tax credits in exchange for the jobs and $109 million in research and development expenditure commitments. Roles include software engineering, computer research, product development, enterprise sales, and operations.
stories.impact: Incremental white-collar job creation in Manhattan supports rental demand for high-income workers, particularly in Union Square submarket and East Village/Gramercy nearby. 650 net new jobs over 5 years (~130/year) is modest for NYC but signals continued tech hub competition and talent gravity; monitor whether other AI/software firms follow or if NYC tax credit offers trigger a wave of subsidy-driven expansions. No direct supply/capital impact, but demand signals favor renter-friendly neighborhoods with transit, dining, and walkability near tech office clusters.

stories.title: Ariel Finalizes Sale of East Harlem Development Site
stories.excerpt: Ariel Property Advisors arranged the $7-million sale of 224-228 E. 118th St., a development site in East Harlem. An Ariel team led by director Howard Raber, along with founding partner Michael A. Tortorici and director Alexander Taic, arranged the transaction for the seller, 118 Standard. The buyers were Joe Katz and Mark Miller of Grun Group. The 79-foot-wide, approximately 7,980-square-foot parcel currently contains a vacant lot and a vacant townhouse. With additional air rights and a light and air easement from an adjacent property, the site offers approximately 45,313 buildable square feet under standard zoning and up to approximately 54,376 buildable square feet with the Universal Affordability Preference. “This transaction reflects renewed developer interest in well-located residential development sites, particularly properties offering scale, zoning flexibility and a clear path to development,” said Raber. “Pricing for Northern Manhattan development sites has strengthened during 2026 as buyers have competed for quality opportunities.” The post Ariel Finalizes Sale of East Harlem Development Site appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Grun Group (Katz, Miller) buys East Harlem development site, 224–228 E. 118th St., for $7M.
Parcel: ~8k SF base + air rights; 45k–54k buildable SF with zoning flexibility.
Ariel broker reports rising Northern Manhattan site pricing and renewed developer competition in 2026.
stories.summary: Ariel Property Advisors brokered a $7-million sale of a 79-foot-wide development site in East Harlem (224–228 E. 118th St.) from 118 Standard to Grun Group (Joe Katz, Mark Miller). The ~7,980-sf parcel with acquired air rights and light/air easement offers 45,313 buildable sf under standard zoning and up to 54,376 sf with Universal Affordability Preference. Ariel notes renewed buyer interest in well-located Northern Manhattan sites with scale and zoning flexibility, with pricing strengthening during 2026.
stories.impact: East Harlem site pricing recovery signals increased developer appetite for Harlem/Upper Manhattan multifamily as gentrification pressures and transit access (1, 2, 5 lines) drive demand. Grun Group entry and pricing strength indicate tighter inventory of entitled/air-rights sites; UAP (affordable housing density bonus) zoning flexibility is now a valuation driver. For Trammell Crow, this flags competition heating up for Manhattan sub-core markets and risk of land cost inflation in Harlem as large developers bid for scale sites ahead of potential regulatory tightening on affordable housing (post-485-x learning).

stories.title: Alfred Equities Buying Starwood’s Former HQ in South Beach for $56M
stories.excerpt: Alfred Equities and entities tied to the May family are under contract to buy the former headquarters of Barry Sternlicht’s Starwood Capital Group in Miami’s South Beach. The New York-based firm, led by Abraham B. Schwartz, plans to pay $55.8 million for the eight-story building at 1601 Washington Avenue, near the corner of 16th Street, near Lincoln Road and Collins Avenue. The 131,220-square-foot asset sits on a 1.4-acre site owned by the City Of Miami Beach. On Nov. 18, the city’s commission will consider waiving its right of first refusal to allow Alfred Equities’ acquisition of the ground lease to close. Under the agreement, Alfred Equities would own the asset alongside family trusts tied to Aryeh and Rivka May, as well as several limited partners, according to filings to Miami Beach. Built in 2002, the building features 106,652 square feet of office space, 28,483 square feet of retail space on the ground floor, and a 493-spot parking garage. The building, called The Lincoln, served as Starwood Capital Group’s headquarters from 2016 and 2022, before the investor moved up the road into a building it developed. The Lincoln became embroiled in controversy. In 2016, Elie Schwartz’s Nightingale Properties purchased the ground lease for $80 million through a crowdfunding platform. Nearly a decade later, Schwartz was sentenced to seven years in federal prison for defrauding investors by misappropriating millions in funds. In 2023, Robert Rivani’s Black Lion went under contract to buy the site for $82 million, The Real Deal reported, though the deal never closed. Two years later, the property fell under the control of lender Granite Point Mortgage Trust after it released a $84.7 million loan through a deed in lieu of foreclosure transaction. Alfred Equities’ pending purchase follows a string of office sales in Miami Beach, as wealthy executives seek offices near their homes. Over the summer, a venture led by Todd Rosenberg‘s Pebb Capital paid at least $70 million
bullets: Alfred Equities/May family buy Starwood Capital HQ, 1601 Washington Ave (South Beach), $55.8M.
131k SF: 106.7k office, 28.5k retail, 493-space garage; 2002-built, ground lease from Miami Beach.
City commission votes Nov. 18 on waiving ROFR; asset vacant since Starwood exit in 2022.
stories.summary: Alfred Equities (led by Abraham B. Schwartz) and entities tied to the May family are under contract to acquire The Lincoln, the former headquarters of Barry Sternlicht's Starwood Capital Group in Miami's South Beach, for $55.8 million. The eight-story asset at 1601 Washington Avenue features 106,652 sf of office, 28,483 sf of retail, and a 493-spot parking garage on 1.4 acres. Built in 2002, it has sat vacant since Starwood vacated in 2022. Miami Beach city commission will vote Nov. 18 on waiving its right of first refusal.
stories.impact: South Beach office-to-residential conversion play signals potential repositioning of trophy office assets into mixed-use or residential in Miami's high-barrier, supply-constrained submarket. Lincoln Road/Collins Avenue location is prime retail and hospitality corridor with strong tourist and high-net-worth resident demand. If Alfred converts significant office footage to luxury rental apartments, it signals confidence in Miami Beach rents and willingness to absorb conversion costs—positive for multifamily demand signals in South Florida, but watch for market saturation if other large office-to-res conversions accelerate. Ground lease structure (city of Miami Beach ownership) adds complexity and may limit value-add upside; monitor lease terms as bellwether for Miami Beach's willingness to cooperate on adaptive reuse.

stories.title: Podcast: Fifth Dimension’s Kate Jarvis on How CRE Asset Managers Can Trust AI Agents
stories.excerpt: Kate Jarvis is the CEO and co-founder of Fifth Dimension, an agentic AI platform built for commercial real estate investment managers, asset managers and brokers. Fifth Dimension structures data from ERPs, CRMs, spreadsheets, PDFs and email into a unified system of record, then deploys prebuilt agents against the most commonly automated workflows in the industry. Prior to founding Fifth Dimension, Jarvis spent roughly a decade working at the intersection of financial services and commercial real estate technology. The company raised $26 million in 2026 and counts Boston Property Group, Realty Income and Peachtree Group among its clients. Kate is based in London. Recorded live from the floor at CREtech NY. stories.title: Forman Capital Lends $51M on North Carolina Shopping Center Project
stories.excerpt: Sagemark Development has landed $50.7 million of construction financing to build a shopping center in North Carolina’s Raleigh-Durham region, Commercial Observer has learned. Forman Capital supplied the loan for the developer’s Adams Crossing project in Sanford, N.C. The 223,153-square-foot development will be anchored by BJ’s Wholesale Club, Academy Sports + Outdoors and Burlington Stores. “Sanford is one of the fastest-growing communities in the Raleigh-Durham region, and the retail market is racing to keep up with the rooftops,” Scott Mehlman, Forman Capital partner and chief investment officer, said in a statement. “With BJ’s, Academy and Burlington anchoring the center, along with a strong mix of national retail, service and restaurant tenants, the project is positioned to perform from the day it opens.” Mehlman added that an existing Walmart next door to Adams Crossing is expected to drive additional foot traffic to the property. He originated the loan with a team that also included Ty Regnier, Mike Rediker and Ben Jacobson in a deal that closed Nov. 13. Located on a 32-acre site at 3350 NC-87 47 miles southwest of Downtown Ralegh, the Adams Crossings project is under construction and slated for completion in late 2027. Other tenants at the 95 percent pre-leased property will include Ulta Beauty, Five Below and Aspen Dental with Olive Garden and Longhorn Steakhouse occupying ground-leased outparcels. “Retail with this caliber of tenants and pre-leasing momentum is exactly where we want to be as a lender,” Jacobson, also a partner at Forman Capital, said in a statement. “Sagemark put together a project that will serve Sanford well for years to come.” Adams Crossing is in a growing area, with Lee County’s population growing 13 percent since 2020 to more than 70,000. The City of Sanford has also approved over 12,000 new residential units over the past five years, according to Forman. Sagemark Development did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Co
bullets: Forman Capital lends $50.7M construction financing for Adams Crossing, Sanford, NC (Raleigh-Durham region).
223k-SF retail center anchored by BJ's, Academy Sports, Burlington; mixed national tenants.
Sanford cited as 'fastest-growing' in RDU; retail market lagging rooftop growth.
stories.summary: Forman Capital provided $50.7 million of construction financing to Sagemark Development for Adams Crossing, a 223,153-sf retail shopping center in Sanford, North Carolina (Raleigh-Durham region). Anchors include BJ's Wholesale Club, Academy Sports + Outdoors, and Burlington Stores, plus a mix of national retail, service, and restaurant tenants. Forman partner Scott Mehlman noted Sanford is one of the RDU region's fastest-growing communities and that the retail market is racing to keep up with residential growth ('rooftops').
stories.impact: Forman's retail construction lending in Raleigh-Durham and explicit call-out of 'rooftops outpacing retail' signals strong residential demand/demographic influx in Sanford submarket. This is a secondary-market population growth flag: residential development is outpacing commercial infrastructure, creating a retail/dining gap and implying strong underlying housing demand momentum. For Trammell Crow, Sanford/RDU entry point warrants site search acceleration in the market—demographic tailwinds and retail underperformance suggest absorption velocity for well-located multifamily. Monitor Sanford residential permitting and job growth as early-stage demand indicators.
